title: Reading the indentation
idea: Indentation decides which if an else belongs to. Learning to read the levels tells you exactly which branch runs. Visible output throughout.

exercises.prompt: In a nested if, how do you tell which 'else' belongs to which 'if'?
options: By how far it is indented - an else lines up with its own if
exercises.explanation: An else belongs to the if at the same indentation level. Lining them up by eye tells you the pairing.
raining is True so we enter the body; have_umbrella is True so the inner if runs: 'Walk with umbrella'.

exercises.prompt: Same code, raining = True, have_umbrella = False. What prints?
exercises.explanation: We are inside the raining branch. The inner if is False, so its else - indented to match the inner if - runs: 'Wait inside'.

exercises.prompt: Same code, raining = False. What prints?
exercises.explanation: The outer if is False, so Python jumps to the outer else (lined up with the outer if): 'Just walk'. The umbrella question is skipped entirely.

exercises.prompt: The outer else lines up with the outer if (no extra indent). What does that tell you?
options: It runs when the OUTER condition is False
It runs when the inner condition is False
exercises.explanation: An else matched to the outer if handles the outer-False case. Indentation is the clue to which if it answers.

exercises.prompt: Arrange these lines so the inner else belongs to the inner if.
exercises.explanation: The inner else is indented to match the inner if, so it answers the umbrella question, not the rain question.

exercises.prompt: Two elses at different indent levels can answer two different ifs in the same nested block.
exercises.explanation: Yes. The deeply indented else answers the inner if; the less indented else answers the outer if.
Two levels deep means 8 spaces (4 for the outer body, 4 more for the inner body). The print belongs to the inner if.
door_open is True, so we enter. light_on is False, so the inner else runs: 'Flip the switch'.

exercises.prompt: Reading nested code, what should you check first to predict the output?
options: The outer condition - if it is False, the whole inner block is skipped
Nothing; just guess the middle line
exercises.explanation: Always read outer-first. A False outer condition means you never even reach the inner question.
